title: Wake up, Bit
story: The lights flicker. Deep in the Ironworks factory, a small maintenance robot called Bit, unit B-17, switches on after a long power cut. The security system WARDEN has locked every door. You are on Bit's radio link, and Bit can only do what your code tells it.
power: ### What is a program? A program is a list of instructions that the computer follows, one after the other, from the top line to the bottom line. Here, your program is the list of things Bit will do. ### print shows something on the screen print is a function: a ready-made command that does a job for you. To use it, you call it: you write its name followed by round brackets, called parentheses ( ). What you put inside the parentheses is what gets shown in the output area. Each print starts a new line. ~~~python print("Good morning") print("Python is ready") ~~~ - Line 1: print receives the text Good morning and writes it as one line of output. - Line 2: Python moves on to the next line and prints Python is ready on a new line. ### Text needs quotes: strings A piece of text is called a string. You wrap it in quotes so Python knows where it starts and stops. Double quotes "..." and single quotes '...' both work, as long as the opening and closing quotes match. The quotes are not printed. Everything between them is printed exactly as written, spaces and punctuation included. ~~~python print("Hello, friend!") print('Single quotes work too.') print(" spaces are kept ") ~~~ ### Comments are notes for humans A line that starts with # (the hash sign) is a comment. Python skips it completely. Everything after a # at the end of a line is ignored too. ~~~python # This line is ignored by Python print("Only this is shown") # a note after the code ~~~ ### Bit's controls The first line of every mission is from robot import *. It means: "bring in all of Bit's controls so I can use them". After it you can call Bit's functions, the same way you call print: - move(): Bit rolls one square forward. - say("text"): Bit says the text in a speech bubble, and it is printed exactly like print would. Each call is one instruction, so three move() lines make Bit roll three squares, from top to bottom in the order you wrote them. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting a quote: print("Hello) stops with a SyntaxError, because Python cannot find where the text ends. - Writing Print or Move with a capital letter. Python is case sensitive: only print and move exist. - Forgetting the parentheses: move alone does nothing. You must write move(). - Typing the text slightly differently from what is asked. A missing letter or a capital counts as a different string.
goal: Make Bit say exactly Bit online, then move it three squares forward onto the exit E.
starter:
from robot import *

# Write your instructions below, one per line
solution:
from robot import *

say("Bit online")
move()
move()
move()
hint: Use say with the text in quotes, then write move() three times, each on its own line.

title: Status report
story: A speaker crackles: WARDEN wants a status report before it lets any unit move. Bit's battery started at 100 and the boot used 37. WARDEN hates guesses, so let Python do the maths.
power: ### Numbers do not need quotes Numbers are written as they are, with no quotes. Python can then calculate with them: + adds and - subtracts. The same characters inside quotes are just text, and Python prints them without calculating anything. ~~~python print(2 + 3) print("2 + 3") print(10 - 4) ~~~ - Line 1: Python first calculates 2 + 3, gets 5, then prints 5. - Line 2: the characters are inside quotes, so this is text: it prints 2 + 3. - Line 3: prints 6. ### Several things in one print You can give print several values separated by commas. Values handed to a function are called arguments. print shows them on one line, with a single space between each one. say works the same way. ~~~python print("Total:", 5 + 5) print("Apples", "and", "pears") print("Sum:", "2 + 2", "=", 2 + 2) ~~~ - Line 1: the text Total:, then the result of 5 + 5: Total: 10. - Line 2: three strings joined with spaces: Apples and pears. - Line 3: the second value is text and the last one is a calculation: Sum: 2 + 2 = 4.
goal: Print exactly three lines: Status report, then Battery: 63 where 63 is calculated by Python from 100 - 37, then Doors: 2 + 2 = 4 where the last number is calculated. Then move Bit to the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

# WARDEN wants a status report
solution:
from robot import *

print("Status report")
print("Battery:", 100 - 37)
print("Doors:", "2 + 2", "=", 2 + 2)
move()
move()
hint: Give print several values separated by commas: text in quotes, calculations without quotes.

title: Memory banks
story: Bit's memory was wiped by the power cut. It does not even know its own name. Before WARDEN's scanner lets it out of the charging bay, Bit must store who it is and keep track of its battery.
power: ### Creating a variable with = A variable is a name that points at a value, so you can use the value later. You create one with =. In Python = does not mean "is equal to". It means "store the value on the right under the name on the left". This is called an assignment. ~~~python name = "Ada" print(name) print("name") ~~~ - Line 1: creates a variable called name holding the string "Ada". - Line 2: no quotes, so Python looks up the variable and prints Ada. - Line 3: with quotes it is just the text name. ### Changing a variable A variable can get a new value at any time; the old one is forgotten. You can also compute a new value from a variable. ~~~python score = 10 print(score) score = 25 print(score) bonus = score + 5 print(bonus) ~~~ - Line 3: score now holds 25. The 10 is gone. - Line 5: Python reads score (25), adds 5 and stores 30 in bonus. ### The four basic types Every value has a type, which says what kind of value it is: - str (string): text, always in quotes, like "Lyon". - int (integer): a whole number, like 42 or -7. No spaces or commas inside: one million is 1000000. - float: a number with a decimal point, like 3.5. Python uses a dot, not a comma. - bool (boolean): True or False, with a capital letter and no quotes. For yes or no facts. ~~~python city = "Paris" rooms = 4 price = 129.99 has_pool = False print(city, rooms, price, has_pool) ~~~ ### Asking Python for the type You never announce the type: Python works it out from the value. type() tells you the type. You can put one function inside another: print(type(x)) first gets the type of x, then prints it. ~~~python rooms = 4 print(type(rooms)) print(type(129.99)) print(type("4")) print(type(True)) ~~~ - Prints <class 'int'>, <class 'float'>, then <class 'str'> because "4" is in quotes, then <class 'bool'>. ### Naming rules Names use lowercase words joined by underscores, like total_price. A name can contain letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit and cannot contain spaces. Names are case sensitive: City and city are two different variables. ### Common mistakes - Writing false or "False". The bool is False, capital F, no quotes. - Putting a number in quotes: "17" is a string, not an int. - Writing 1,000 or 1 000 for a number. - Using a variable before creating it stops the program with a NameError.
goal: Create name holding the text Bit, unit holding the whole number 17, temperature holding 21.5 and awake holding True. Make Bit say all four in that order with one say, then print the type of temperature. Then set battery to 100, move three squares to the exit, take 3 away with battery = battery - 3 and say Battery followed by its value.
solution:
from robot import *

name = "Bit"
unit = 17
temperature = 21.5
awake = True
say(name, unit, temperature, awake)
print(type(temperature))
battery = 100
move()
move()
move()
battery = battery - 3
say("Battery", battery)
hint: Text goes in quotes, numbers and True do not; print(type(temperature)) shows the type.
test:
assert 'name' in dir() and name == 'Bit', "Store the text Bit in a variable called name."
assert 'unit' in dir() and type(unit) == int and unit == 17, "unit should be the whole number 17, without quotes."
assert 'temperature' in dir() and type(temperature) == float, "temperature should be the decimal number 21.5."
assert 'awake' in dir() and awake is True, "awake should be the bool True: capital T, no quotes."
assert 'battery' in dir() and battery == 97, "battery should go from 100 down to 97 with battery = battery - 3."

title: The time lock
story: The bay door has a time lock. Its terminal shows how many minutes are left, but the keypad wants hours and minutes: the hours times 100, plus the minutes. The number is different every time WARDEN resets the lock.
power: ### The basic operators An operator is a symbol that calculates with the values on each side of it. - + adds, - subtracts. - * (the star) multiplies. Python never uses x for multiplication. - / divides, and always gives a float, even when the result is whole. ~~~python print(7 + 2) print(7 - 2) print(7 * 2) print(7 / 2) print(8 / 2) ~~~ - The last line prints 4.0, not 4: / always gives a float. ### Whole division // and remainder % Two operators work as a pair when you split something into whole groups: - // (floor division) divides and keeps only the whole part. 17 // 5 is 3: 5 fits into 17 three whole times. - % (modulo) gives what is left over. 17 % 5 is 2: 3 times 5 is 15, and 17 minus 15 leaves 2. ~~~python eggs = 17 boxes = eggs // 6 left = eggs % 6 print(boxes, "full boxes and", left, "eggs left") ~~~ ### Converting minutes into hours There are 60 minutes in an hour, so // 60 gives the whole hours and % 60 gives the minutes that do not make a full hour. ~~~python total_minutes = 200 hours = total_minutes // 60 minutes = total_minutes % 60 print(hours, minutes) ~~~ - 60 fits into 200 three times, so hours is 3. 3 hours are 180 minutes, so minutes is 20. Prints 3 20. ### Terminals and doors Two new controls for Bit: - scan(): when Bit stands on a terminal (a digit on the map), it reads the terminal and gives back its value. Store it: total = scan(). Scanning is free, it uses no battery. - unlock(code): types the code into the door in front of Bit. A wrong code sounds the alarm and the run fails. ### Common mistakes - Using / when you want a whole number. Use // for whole groups. - Mixing up // ("how many whole times") and % ("what is left over"). - Writing x for multiplication. Use *.
goal: Walk onto the terminal, scan the minutes left, and compute the hours and the leftover minutes. Unlock door A with hours * 100 + minutes (200 minutes give 320), then reach the exit. The minutes are different on every map.
solution:
from robot import *

move()
total = scan()
hours = total // 60
minutes = total % 60
move()
unlock(hours * 100 + minutes)
move()
move()
hint: hours is the total with // 60, minutes is the total with % 60; Python multiplies before it adds.

title: Power grid
story: The next door runs on salvaged battery cells. Its keypad wants the power per circuit: 2 to the power of the number of cells, shared between the circuits, rounded to 2 decimals. Two terminals give the cell count and the circuit count.
power: ### Powers with ** ** (two stars) raises to a power: 3 ** 2 is 3 times 3, and 2 ** 5 is 2 multiplied by itself 5 times. ~~~python print(3 ** 2) print(2 ** 5) ~~~ ### Order of operations and parentheses Python follows the same priority rules as maths: ** first, then *, /, // and %, then + and -. Operators of the same priority run from left to right. Parentheses force a part to be calculated first. ~~~python print(2 + 3 * 4) print((2 + 3) * 4) print(2 ** 3 / 4) days_left = 100 % 30 // 7 print(days_left) ~~~ - Line 1: 3 * 4 first (12), then plus 2: 14. - Line 2: the parentheses go first (5), then times 4: 20. - Line 3: 2 ** 3 first (8), then divided by 4: 2.0. - Line 4: same priority, so left to right: 100 % 30 is 10, then 10 // 7 is 1. ### Rounding with round round(number, digits) rounds a number to the given number of decimal places. It takes two arguments, separated by a comma. ~~~python price = 10 / 3 print(price) print(round(price, 2)) ~~~ - price is 3.3333333333333335 (computers store decimals with tiny imprecision). Rounded to 2 decimals it prints 3.33.
goal: Scan terminal 1 (the cells) and terminal 2 (the circuits). Compute 2 ** cells / circuits rounded to 2 decimals, make Bit say Power: followed by that value, unlock door A with it and reach the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
cells = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
cells = scan()
move()
circuits = scan()
power = round(2 ** cells / circuits, 2)
say("Power:", power)
unlock(power)
move()
move()
hint: ** runs before /, so 2 ** cells / circuits needs no parentheses; wrap it all in round(..., 2).

title: The garbled nameplate
story: Two doors guard the bay's exit. Their codes are the name on a rusty nameplate, but the terminal reads it back garbled: random capitals and stray spaces. Door A wants the name in title case, door B in lower case.
power: ### Methods: tools attached to a string A method is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot after the value: text.upper(). The empty parentheses are still required. A string method never changes the original string: it gives back a new string, which you usually store in a variable. - .strip() removes spaces at the start and the end (not in the middle). - .upper() makes every letter capital, .lower() makes every letter small. - .title() makes the first letter of each word capital and the rest small. ~~~python raw = " alan TURING " print("[" + raw.strip() + "]") print(raw.upper()) print(raw.lower()) print(raw.title()) print("[" + raw + "]") ~~~ - Line 2: + between strings glues them together. The brackets show the edges: [alan TURING]. - Lines 3 to 5: ALAN TURING , alan turing , Alan Turing . - Line 6: [ alan TURING ]: raw itself never changed. ### Chaining methods Each method returns a new string, so you can call another method on the result straight away. Python works from left to right. ~~~python raw = " alan TURING " clean = raw.strip().title() print(clean) ~~~ - raw.strip() gives "alan TURING", then .title() on that gives "Alan Turing". ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the parentheses: raw.strip without () does not run the method. - Expecting raw.strip() alone to change raw. Store the result: clean = raw.strip().
goal: Scan the nameplate and strip its spaces. Unlock door A with the title case version and door B with the lower case version. On the exit, say Cleared: glued with + to the name in capitals, like Cleared: NORTH VENT.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
raw = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
raw = scan()
clean = raw.strip()
unlock(clean.title())
move()
unlock(clean.lower())
move()
move()
say("Cleared: " + clean.upper())
hint: Store raw.strip() in a variable first, then call .title(), .lower() and .upper() on it.

title: Serial cutter
story: WARDEN's last checkpoint in the bay builds its codes from a three word phrase on a terminal. Door A wants the first three letters of the phrase followed by its last letter. Door B wants the first letter of each word followed by the phrase's length.
power: ### Indexing: one character at a time Each character in a string has a position number called an index. Counting starts at 0, not 1. You read one character with square brackets: word[0]. Negative numbers count from the end: -1 is the last character. A slice word[start:stop] takes several characters, from start up to but not including stop. len(word) gives the number of characters. ~~~python word = "Python" print(word[0]) print(word[1]) print(word[-1]) print(word[0:3]) print(len(word)) ~~~ - Positions are P=0, y=1, t=2, h=3, o=4, n=5. Prints P, y, n, then Pyt (positions 0, 1 and 2), then 6. ### Splitting text into words .split() cuts a string at every run of spaces and gives back the pieces as a list: several values in order, inside square brackets. You read a list item with an index too. Each item is a string, so you can index it again: parts[1][0] means "item 1, then its character 0". ~~~python city = "new york city" parts = city.split() print(parts) print(parts[1]) print(parts[1][0]) print(parts[0][0] + parts[2][0]) ~~~ - parts is ['new', 'york', 'city']. Item 1 is york, its first character is y, and n glued to c gives nc. ### f-strings: putting values inside text An f-string has the letter f just before the opening quote. Inside it, anything in curly braces { } is replaced by its value. You can calculate and call methods inside the braces. ~~~python name = "Ada" age = 36 print(f"{name} is {age} years old") print(f"In 4 years: {age + 4}") print(f"[{name.upper()}]") ~~~ - Prints Ada is 36 years old, In 4 years: 40, then [ADA]. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the f before the quote: the braces are then printed as they are. - Counting from 1. The first character or item is at index 0.
goal: Scan the phrase. Unlock door A with its first three characters (a slice) glued to its last character (index -1). Split it into words and unlock door B with an f-string made of the first letter of each of the three words, then the length of the whole phrase (for steel gate north that is sgn16). Reach the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
text = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
text = scan()
unlock(text[0:3] + text[-1])
move()
words = text.split()
unlock(f"{words[0][0]}{words[1][0]}{words[2][0]}{len(text)}")
move()
move()
hint: text[0:3] is the slice, words[1][0] is the first letter of the second word, len(text) counts every character, spaces included.

title: WARDEN's quiz
story: At the bay's exit WARDEN asks its questions out loud: Bit's radio receives each answer as one line of input. A password, two numbers and a rate. Three doors stand in a row, and WARDEN expects real maths, not glued text.
power: ### input reads one line input() waits for one line of text and gives it back as a string. You usually store it in a variable. In a mission, the lines are listed under the map: the first input() receives the first line, the second input() the second line, and so on. Each call reads exactly one line, so to read two values you call it twice. ~~~text name = input() # reads the first line, say Ada age = input() # reads the second line, say 36 ~~~ ### A prompt tells the user what to type You can put a string inside the parentheses: input("Which city? "). It is shown before the user types, as a question. It is called a prompt and it does not change the value that is read. ### The trap: input always gives text Even when the line contains digits, input() returns a string. And + between two strings glues them. Here are the values two input() calls would give for the lines 12 and 30: ~~~python a = "12" b = "30" print(a + b) print(type(a)) ~~~ - Prints 1230, not 42, then <class 'str'>: the proof that it is text. ### Converting text into numbers int(text) turns a string of digits into a whole number, negative numbers included. float(text) turns text like "2.5" into a decimal number. str(value) goes the other way and turns a number into text. ~~~python quantity = int("4") price = float("2.5") print(quantity * price) print(int("-5") + 1) print(str(7) + "7") ~~~ - Prints 10.0, -4, then 77. You can wrap the conversion directly around input(). Python runs the inner function first (read the line), then the outer one (convert it): ~~~text age = int(input("Your age: ")) print(f"You will be {age + 1} next year") ~~~ ### Common mistakes - Forgetting int(), so + glues text instead of adding. - Converting text that is not a whole number: int("abc") or int("2.5") stops with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10. Use float() for decimals. - Calling input() once and expecting several lines. - Mismatched parentheses in int(input()): every opening one needs a closing one.
goal: Read four lines: a password, two whole numbers and a decimal rate. Unlock door A with the password in capitals, door B with the sum of the two numbers, and door C with the rate times 2. Then reach the exit. The answers change on every map.
solution:
from robot import *

password = input()
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
rate = float(input())
unlock(password.upper())
move()
unlock(a + b)
move()
unlock(rate * 2)
move()
move()
hint: Wrap each number in int(input()) or float(input()), one call per line.

title: The hot fork
story: Bit rolls into the Corridors. At the first fork, one way leads on and the other ends in a hole where the floor melted. A terminal shows the furnace temperature: at 100 degrees or more the north corridor is the burnt one and Bit must go south, otherwise north is safe.
power: ### Comparisons give True or False A comparison checks two values and gives back a bool: True or False. Python has six comparison operators: - == equal to (two equals signs; one = is for assignment) - != not equal to - < less than, <= less than or equal to - > greater than, >= greater than or equal to ~~~python age = 17 print(age >= 18) print(age < 18) print(age == 17) print(age != 17) ~~~ - Prints False, True, True, False. ### if: run a block only when a condition is true Write if, a condition, then a colon :. The lines that belong to the if come underneath, indented by 4 spaces. This indented group is a block. Python runs it only when the condition is True. The first line that is no longer indented is outside the block and always runs. ~~~python total = 65 if total >= 50: print("Free shipping!") print("Thanks for your order") print("Done") ~~~ - Both indented lines run because 65 >= 50. Change 65 to 30: only Done is printed. ### else: the other case else: (with a colon and no condition) gives a block to run when the condition is False. Exactly one of the two blocks runs. ~~~python stock = 3 if stock > 0: print("In stock") else: print("Sold out") ~~~ ### Turning Bit turn_left() and turn_right() turn Bit a quarter turn on the spot. Facing east (right on the map), turn_left() makes Bit face north (up) and turn_right() makes it face south (down). ### Common mistakes - Writing = instead of == in a condition: a SyntaxError. - Forgetting the colon at the end of if or else. - Wrong indentation: all lines of a block must be indented by the same amount.
goal: Scan the temperature, then move to the fork. If it is 100 or more, turn right (south), else turn left (north). Then move twice to the exit. The temperature changes on every map, so a fixed path falls in a hole.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
temp = scan()
move()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
temp = scan()
move()
if temp >= 100:
    turn_right()
else:
    turn_left()
move()
move()
hint: Use if temp >= 100: with an indented turn_right(), and else: with an indented turn_left().

title: The alarm junction
story: A three way junction. Two terminals tell Bit whether WARDEN's alarm is on and the threat level. Two of the three corridors are trapped on every map, and which ones depends on both readings.
power: ### elif: a chain of choices elif means "else if". It adds another condition, checked only when the ones above were false. Python checks from top to bottom and runs only the first branch that is true, then skips the rest. A final else catches everything left over. So the order matters: put the strictest test first. ~~~python age = 12 if age >= 65: print("Senior ticket") elif age >= 18: print("Adult ticket") elif age >= 4: print("Child ticket") else: print("Free") ~~~ - 12 >= 65 and 12 >= 18 are false, 12 >= 4 is true: prints Child ticket and skips the rest. If age >= 4 came first, a 70 year old would get a child ticket. ### and, or, not and is true only when both sides are true. or is true when at least one side is true. not flips True into False and back. ~~~python temp = 22 raining = False if temp > 18 and not raining: print("Picnic time") if temp < 0 or raining: print("Stay inside") ~~~ - temp > 18 is true and not raining is true, so it prints Picnic time. The or has two false sides, so the second block does not run. ### Blocks inside blocks A block can contain another if. Indent it one more level (8 spaces). ~~~python door = "open" level = 3 if door == "open": if level > 2: print("Open, but dangerous") else: print("Open and safe") ~~~ ### Common mistakes - Checking in the wrong order, so a lower test catches values meant for a higher one. - Forgetting the colon at the end of elif or else.
goal: Scan alarm (True or False) on terminal 1 and level on terminal 2, then move to the junction. First say All quiet if the alarm is off or the level is below 3, else say Danger. Then: if the alarm is on and the level is 5 or more, go north (left); elif the level is below 5, go south (right); otherwise go straight on. Move twice to reach the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
alarm = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
alarm = scan()
move()
level = scan()
move()
if not alarm or level < 3:
    say("All quiet")
else:
    say("Danger")
if alarm and level >= 5:
    turn_left()
elif level < 5:
    turn_right()
move()
move()
hint: Write the say part and the turning part as two separate if statements; going straight needs no turn at all.

title: The long corridor
story: The corridor ahead stretches into the dark, and WARDEN changes its length every time the walls shift. A terminal at its start knows how many squares it is. The radio team also wants the warning lights reported: there is one every 3 squares, starting at square 0.
power: ### Looping over a list of items A list is several values in square brackets, separated by commas. A for loop is written for name in collection:, then an indented block. On each round, called an iteration, Python puts the next item into the loop variable and runs the block. ~~~python for fruit in ["apple", "kiwi", "pear"]: print("I like", fruit) print("End of the list") ~~~ - fruit is "apple", then "kiwi", then "pear". The last line is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop. Use Step through to watch fruit change. ### range: counting numbers range(stop) produces the whole numbers from 0 up to, but not including, stop. range(3) gives 0, 1, 2: three numbers, so the block runs 3 times. ~~~python for i in range(3): print("Round", i) ~~~ ### range with a start and a step range(start, stop) starts at start and still stops just before stop. A third value, the step, sets how much to add each time: range(start, stop, step). To count from 1 to 5 included, write range(1, 6). ~~~python for day in range(1, 6): print(f"Day {day} of 5") for n in range(0, 20, 5): print(n) ~~~ - day takes 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. n takes 0, 5, 10 and 15: 20 is excluded. ### Using the loop variable in a calculation The loop variable is an ordinary variable: you can calculate with it and combine it with other variables, such as a number you scanned or read. ~~~python size = 4 for i in range(1, 4): print(f"{i} box(es) of {size} = {i * size} items") ~~~ ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the colon at the end of the for line. - Forgetting to indent the lines that should repeat, or indenting a line that should run only once. - Off by one: range(1, 10) stops at 9. To include 10, write range(1, 11).
goal: Scan the corridor length. With a for loop over range(0, length, 3), say Light at and each number, like Light at 3. Then, with a second for loop counting from 1 to the length included, move one square and say Step and the number each round. Bit ends on the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
length = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
length = scan()
for i in range(0, length, 3):
    say(f"Light at {i}")
for i in range(1, length + 1):
    move()
    say(f"Step {i}")
hint: range(1, length + 1) includes length itself; put both move() and say() inside the second loop.

title: The route card
story: A terminal hands Bit a route card: a string of letters. F means one square forward, L a left turn, R a right turn. The corridors twist differently on every map, and the door at the end wants the number of squares Bit actually moved.
power: ### Looping over a string A string is also a collection: of characters. A for loop over a string gives one character per round. ~~~python for letter in "Hey": print(letter) ~~~ - letter is "H", then "e", then "y". ### Keeping a running total A common pattern: create a variable before the loop, then update it inside the loop. total = total + n means "take the current total, add n, store the result back in total". ~~~python total = 0 for n in range(1, 5): total = total + n print("after adding", n, "total is", total) print("Final:", total) ~~~ - total goes 1, 3, 6, 10. After the loop it prints Final: 10. ### A decision inside a loop The block of a loop can contain an if. Indent it inside the loop, and its own block one level more. ~~~python count = 0 for c in "banana": if c == "a": count = count + 1 print(count, "letters a") ~~~ ### Common mistakes - Putting the starting value of the total inside the loop, which resets it on every round. - Comparing with = instead of ==.
goal: Scan the route card, then follow it letter by letter with a for loop: F moves, L turns left, R turns right. Count the squares moved in a running total that starts at 0, unlock door A with that count, and move twice to the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
route = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
route = scan()
steps = 0
for c in route:
    if c == "F":
        move()
        steps = steps + 1
    elif c == "L":
        turn_left()
    else:
        turn_right()
unlock(steps)
move()
move()
hint: Inside for c in route:, use if, elif and else on c; set steps = 0 before the loop, not inside it.

title: The dark hall
story: The power fails again and the hall goes dark. Bit cannot see how long it is, only whether it is standing on the exit yet. Every action drains its battery, so a loop that never stops will leave Bit stranded. Coins lie on the floor, and the radio team wants a beacon report.
power: ### while: repeat as long as a condition is true for is perfect when you know what to go through. while repeats until something happens. You write while, a condition and a colon, then an indented block. Before each round Python checks the condition. If it is True, the block runs and Python checks again. As soon as it is False, the loop ends. ~~~python count = 3 while count > 0: print(count) count = count - 1 print("Lift off") ~~~ - Prints 3, 2, 1, then count is 0, 0 > 0 is false, and it prints Lift off. ### The infinite loop Something inside the loop must change the condition. If count never went down, the loop would never end. This is an infinite loop; the page stops it after 3 seconds. For Bit it is worse: every move(), turn or say() uses one unit of battery, so a robot stuck in a loop drains its battery and the run fails. Bit's sensors are free: at_exit() is True when Bit stands on the exit, and here() names the square under Bit, like "coin" or "floor". pick() picks up the coin Bit stands on. ### Shortcuts: += and -= i += 1 means exactly i = i + 1, and count -= 1 means count = count - 1. ~~~python i = 1 while i <= 5: print("Item", i) i += 1 print("i ended at", i) ~~~ ### Testing "is a multiple of" with % A number is a multiple of 3 exactly when dividing it by 3 leaves nothing: n % 3 == 0. ~~~python n = 1 while n <= 6: if n % 2 == 0: print(n, "is even") else: print(n, "is odd") n += 1 ~~~ ### Checking the combined case first When a number can match two rules, check the combined rule first, because an if / elif chain runs only the first true branch. A multiple of both 2 and 3 is a multiple of 6. ~~~python n = 1 while n <= 7: if n % 6 == 0: print(n, "both") elif n % 2 == 0: print(n, "two") elif n % 3 == 0: print(n, "three") else: print(n) n += 1 ~~~ - If the n % 2 test came first, 6 would print 6 two and never reach the combined test. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting to update the counter, which makes an infinite loop. - Putting the update inside an if or else block, so it only happens in some rounds. - Testing a single rule before the combined rule in an elif chain.
goal: Start steps at 0. While Bit is not on the exit: move, add 1 to steps with +=, pick up a coin if Bit stands on one, then say the step number and beacon on multiples of 6, or the number and light on other multiples of 3 (like 6 beacon, 3 light). At the end say Exit after, the steps, and squares.
hint: while not at_exit(): keeps going until the exit; test steps % 6 before steps % 3.

title: The sinkhole run
story: The last corridor of the section has a sinkhole, and it is in a different place each time WARDEN shakes the floor. The way out is the side passage to the north, just before the hole. Coins are scattered along the way and Bit must collect every one.
power: ### break and continue Two keywords control a loop from inside. break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current round and goes back to the condition check. In a while loop, make sure the counter moves forward before a continue, otherwise the same value is tested forever. ~~~python n = 0 while n < 10: n += 1 if n % 2 == 0: continue if n > 7: break print(n) print("stopped at", n) ~~~ - n goes up at the start of each round, before any continue. - Even numbers hit continue and are never printed. - When n reaches 9, break ends the loop. It prints 1, 3, 5, 7, then stopped at 9. ### while True and break while True: never stops by itself: the condition is always true. That is fine as long as a break inside it is sure to happen. For Bit, the robot equivalent of moving the counter forward is move(): if Bit never moves, it never reaches the hole and the loop never ends. ~~~python fuel = 5 while True: fuel -= 2 print("fuel", fuel) if fuel < 0: break print("empty") ~~~ The sensor front() names the square in front of Bit, like "hole", "wall" or "floor". It is free. ### Common mistakes - Using continue before the counter update (or before move()): nothing changes and the loop spins forever. - A while True loop with no reachable break.
goal: Start coins at 0. In a while True loop: break if the square in front is a hole, otherwise move; if there is no coin under Bit, continue; else pick it up and add 1 to coins. After the loop turn left, move twice to the exit and say Coins: and the count.
solution:
from robot import *

coins = 0
while True:
    if front() == "hole":
        break
    move()
    if here() != "coin":
        continue
    pick()
    coins += 1
turn_left()
move()
move()
say("Coins:", coins)
hint: Test front() == "hole" before moving, and put move() before the continue so Bit always makes progress.
